Report_ID: Children’s dermatology-related quality of life (post-intervention CDLQI total score)
Title: The Effects of a School-Based Atopy Care Program for School-Aged Children
Author: Hosihn Ryu and Youngjin Lee
Comment: M_diff was computed as group_2 mean minus group_1 mean (4.3 - 4.6 = -0.3), so its orientation is positive when the SACP yields lower/better CDLQI scores than control. SE_diff was computed from the explicitly reported SDs and analyzed group sizes as sqrt(4.5^2/32 + 5.0^2/66) = 1.0058. The supplied table formatting is corrupted; 0.92 appears in the between-group test-statistic area and p=.36 is explicit, but the precise named test/statistic column cannot be established with complete confidence, so statistic_type is recorded as other. The paper explicitly reports only the per-item 0-to-3 response range, not a fixed total-score range; total-scale minimum and maximum are therefore left null.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Test group participating in the school-based atopy care program (SACP)') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
Study Environment: Four elementary schools in Seoul; group education delivered in school health management offices
Medium: In-person school-based multidisciplinary group education supplemented by school-nurse case management
Content length: Six 40-min group education lessons; case-management interviews were also provided
Topic of Content: Atopic dermatitis understanding, treatment, stress, parent-child relationships, nutrition, skin care, itching/scratching management, bathing, and moisturizing
interaction_type: Group education for parents and/or children plus individual face-to-face and telephone case-management contacts
Participant type: School-aged children aged 8 to 12 years with atopic dermatitis and their parents/guardians
Recruitment source: Four elementary schools in Seoul; posters and written contact with parents of children identified as having atopic dermatitis
Outcome measurement: CDLQI: 10 items about the past week, each scored on a four-point Likert-type scale from 0 (not at all) to 3 (very much); completed by parents through discussion with their children; higher total scores indicate greater negative impact and worse quality of life
Outcome variable: Children’s dermatology-related quality of life (post-intervention CDLQI total score)
outcome_family: dermatology-related quality of life (DLQI and eligible infant/child/family variants)
effect_direction: Lower CDLQI scores are better; orient the effect so positive favors group education

Title: Pediatric Atopic Eczema: The Impact of an Educational Intervention
Author: Grillo et al.
Comment: M_diff was computed as intervention minus control (1.75 − 7.08 = −5.33), following the required group_2 − group_1 convention. Because lower CDLQI scores are better, the negative raw difference favors group education; synthesis must reverse the sign to make positive values favor intervention. The Results state 23 total participants in this age stratum, but arm-specific and final week-12 analyzed Ns are not reported, so N fields are null.; ANOVA: missing F-value or group sizes
domain: Pediatric atopic eczema / dermatology-related quality of life
Topic of Content: Atopic eczema, triggers, investigations, skin care, topical corticosteroids, infection, wet wraps, additional treatments, and complementary therapies
Participant type: Children aged 5–16 years with atopic eczema and their parents/caregivers
Recruitment source: Local newspaper advertising, audio/visual media coverage, and referrals from hospital dermatologists and immunologists
Outcome measurement: Children's Dermatology Life Quality Index (CDLQI), used for children aged 5–16 years; higher scores indicate greater quality-of-life impairment
outcome_family: dermatology-related quality of life (DLQI and eligible infant/child/family variants)
effect_direction: Lower CDLQI scores are better; orient the effect so positive favors group education

Title: The significance of structured parental educational intervention on childhood atopic dermatitis: a randomized controlled trial
Author: N. Pustišek et al.
Comment: M_diff was computed as group_2_mean − group_1_mean = control − intervention = 13.09 − 10.27 = 2.82 so that a positive value favors group education, as required by the synthesis plan. SE_diff was computed from the explicitly reported SDs and final analysed group sizes: sqrt(5.584^2/64 + 5.759^2/64) = 1.003. The reported t statistic (-2.820) uses the table's intervention-minus-control direction and is therefore negative. No publication year or fixed FDLQI scale range was explicitly stated in the supplied paper text.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Intervention group: structured parental educational programme plus usual medical treatment') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
domain: Pediatric atopic dermatitis; dermatology-related family quality of life
Study Environment: Outpatient Unit of Pediatric Dermatology, Children’s Hospital Zagreb
Topic of Content: Atopic dermatitis causes, aggravating factors, nutrition, diagnostic tests, skin care and treatment, disease effects on child and family quality of life, relaxation methods, topical treatment, moist bandages, and skin care
interaction_type: Group lecture and practical workshop delivered by a dermatologist and nurse to groups of 5–8 participants, with an educational booklet and corticosteroid-use diary
Participant type: Parents of children aged 3 months to 7 years with moderate or severe atopic dermatitis
Recruitment source: Parents of children first seen at the Outpatient Unit of Pediatric Dermatology, Children’s Hospital Zagreb, between June and December 2014
Outcome measurement: Croatian version of the Family Dermatology Life Quality Index (FDLQI), total score
outcome_family: dermatology-related quality of life (DLQI and eligible infant/child/family variants)
effect_direction: Lower FDLQI scores are better; orient the effect so positive favors group education

Report_ID: Dermatology-related quality of life in infants/young children (IDQOL/IDLQI change from baseline to 6 months)
Title: Therapeutic patient education in children with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis: A multicenter randomized controlled trial in China
Author: Liang et al.
Comment: Table 2 reports P<.05 rather than an exact P value, so p_value is left null. The narrative reports P=.030 for the 6-month improvement comparison, while Table 2 gives P<.05; the exact narrative P is retained only in the evidence quote because the row is anchored to the Table 2 △6M statistics. M_diff is left null to avoid creating a raw group_2−group_1 contrast whose sign would conflict with the synthesis convention that positive effects favor education. This age-stratified comparison is dependent on the CDLQI comparison from the same trial.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Therapeutic patient education plus conventional treatment') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
Design Type: Multicenter open-label parallel-group randomized controlled trial
Medium: In-person multidisciplinary group education with take-home video and printed materials
Topic of Content: Long-term atopic dermatitis management, food allergy, psychological interventions/family happiness, skin care, and emollient use
interaction_type: Group lectures followed by consultation and discussion with instructors
Participant type: Children aged 2–4 years with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis and their parents
Recruitment source: Six Chinese hospitals: five children’s hospitals and one general hospital
Outcome measurement: Change in Infants’ Dermatitis Quality of Life Index score from baseline to 6 months; larger positive change values represent a greater fall in impairment score

outcome_family: dermatology-related quality of life (DLQI and eligible infant/child/family variants)
